meta.disclaimer: Every customer, wallet and transaction in this snapshot is synthetic. Nothing here is filed with FINTRAC. Indicators are not findings that money laundering occurred.

rules.name: Large cash receipts reached the reporting threshold
rules.description: Cash received for one conductor totalled CAD 10,000 or more in a single receipt or across a consecutive 24-hour window. This is a Large Cash Transaction Report observation. It is not, by itself, a ground for suspicion.

rules.name: International electronic funds transfers reached the reporting threshold
rules.description: International electronic funds transfers in one direction totalled CAD 10,000 or more in a single transfer or across 24 hours. Domestic wires are out of scope. This is an EFTR observation, not an indicator of suspicion.

rules.name: Cash receipts structured below the large-cash threshold
rules.description: Three or more cash receipts each stay under CAD 10,000 and at or above CAD 2,000, and together reach the threshold inside 48 hours. The pattern is an indicator that the amount may have been broken up. It is not proof of structuring, and a 24-hour total that itself crosses CAD 10,000 is also an LCTR under AML-FI-001.

rules.name: Rapid movement of funds from one rail to another
rules.description: Value arrives as cash or by electronic transfer and a substantial share leaves on a different rail — commonly virtual currency — within a few hours. Virtual-currency pass-through on a single rail remains AML-VC-003.

rules.name: Several customers place sub-threshold cash with one beneficiary
rules.description: Three or more customers deliver cash below CAD 10,000 to the same beneficiary inside 24 hours, and the combined amount reaches the threshold. Each conductor may stay under the LCTR line. The pattern is the multi-party form of smurfing and is an indicator, not a finding of fact.

rules.name: Name resembles an entry on the sample sanctions list
rules.description: The customer, a beneficiary, a third party, or a travel-rule name on the transaction scores at or above the similarity line against the bundled fictional sanctions list. Token order and small spelling differences still match. This is not a legal designation.

rules.name: Name resembles an entry on the sample PEP list
rules.description: A party name scores at or above the similarity line against the bundled fictional politically-exposed-person list. A PEP match is a reason for enhanced review. It is not an indication that a report must be filed.

rules.name: Trade payment diverges from the declared goods value
rules.description: A payment tagged with trade details has an invoice value that differs from the declared goods value by at least 25 percent, and the invoice is at least CAD 1,000. The pattern is the over- and under-invoicing form of trade-based laundering. It is an indicator, not a finding.

rules.name: MSB cash-in followed by payouts to several beneficiaries
rules.description: A customer whose business is money services or remittance receives at least CAD 5,000 in cash and, within 24 hours, pays three or more distinct beneficiaries on a non-cash rail. Multiple third-party payouts are an MSB typology indicator.

rules.name: Casino chips purchased and largely redeemed with minimal play
rules.description: Chips of at least CAD 3,000 are purchased and recorded gaming activity is at most 20 percent of that buy-in, and the value is redeemed to a third party or leaves by wire or virtual currency. Minimal play is a casino typology indicator, not a finding that the chips laundered funds.

rules.name: Sample terrorist-property list matched a party on the transaction
rules.description: A party name matches the bundled fictional terrorist-property sample. On a real listed-person match, a Terrorist Property Report would have to be considered for property in the reporting entity's possession or control. This sample hit does not create that duty and is not an STR indicator by itself.

rules.name: International EFT is missing travel-rule originator or beneficiary fields
rules.description: An international electronic funds transfer at or above CAD 1,000 does not carry the originator and beneficiary name, account, address, and beneficiary institution the travel rule expects. Domestic wires are out of scope. A gap is a record defect. It is not, by itself, suspicion.

rules.name: Rapid inbound activity from multiple distinct wallets
rules.description: Superseded by v2.1, which tightened the sender count from 8 to 5 after tuning against the Q1 alert population.  Retained so that cases assessed before 2026-06-01 remain reproducible.

rules.name: Rapid inbound activity from multiple distinct wallets
rules.description: Multiple incoming virtual-currency transfers from several distinct sending wallets within a short period.

rules.name: Repeated receipts accumulating just below the reporting threshold
rules.description: Several receipts aggregate to a value approaching but not reaching the LVCTR threshold.  Threshold proximity alone is not proof of structuring; it is one input within a holistic review.

rules.name: Rapid pass-through of received virtual currency
rules.description: Value received is moved out again almost immediately, leaving little or no balance behind - consistent with the account being used as a conduit rather than for its stated purpose.

rules.name: Receipt volume far above the customer's own baseline
rules.description: Superseded by v2.0. Retained so cases assessed before 2026-07-01 remain reproducible with the parameters that were in force.

rules.name: Receipt volume far above the customer's own baseline
rules.description: Value received in the last 24 hours is a large multiple of the customer's average *active-day* volume. v1.0 compared against an all-days average, which is near zero for any low-frequency customer and made ordinary deposits look like 30x deviations; it alerted on roughly a third of the book. v2.0 also requires a minimum number of active days before the comparator is considered meaningful.

guidance.title: Large virtual currency transaction threshold
guidance.text: A large virtual currency transaction report is about virtual currency received, not about suspicion. The public reporting line is CAD 10,000 or more in virtual currency in the course of a single transaction. Receiving is the direction that matters for this report. Sending virtual currency onward does not, by itself, create the same large-receipt report. The obligation is arithmetic. It is a different decision from whether anyone has reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering or terrorist financing.

guidance.title: The 24-hour rule for aggregation
guidance.text: Several smaller transactions can add up to one reportable amount when they occur inside a consecutive 24-hour window and they are related. Public guidance describes grouping by the person who conducts the transactions, by the beneficiary, or by the person on whose behalf the transactions are made. The window is rolling and consecutive, not a calendar day. Once a set of transactions has been reported together, those same transactions are not aggregated again into a second report of the same kind. Aggregation is how a reporting threshold is reached. It does not, by itself, mean the activity is suspicious.

guidance.title: Large cash transaction reports
guidance.text: A large cash transaction report applies when a reporting entity receives CAD 10,000 or more in cash in a single transaction, or when cash receipts that belong together reach that amount inside 24 hours. Cash means currency and coins. A wire, an electronic transfer, and virtual currency are not cash for this report. Crossing the line creates a reporting observation. It is not a finding that the cash is proceeds of crime, and it is not the same document as a suspicious transaction report.

guidance.title: Electronic funds transfer reports
guidance.text: An electronic funds transfer report is aimed at international electronic funds transfers of CAD 10,000 or more, including transfers that only reach that amount once they are added together under the 24-hour rule. The transfer has to cross Canada's border. A domestic wire, including payroll between Canadian accounts, is outside this report. Direction matters: incoming and outgoing international transfers are not mixed into one total. As with the cash and virtual-currency thresholds, the report records that the line was reached. It does not record suspicion.

guidance.title: Suspicious transaction reports and reasonable grounds
guidance.text: A suspicious transaction report is filed when there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a transaction, or an attempted transaction, is related to the commission or attempted commission of a money laundering or terrorist activity financing offence. Reasonable grounds to suspect is a lower bar than proof, and it is also more than a hunch. Indicators are clues that can support that judgement when they are considered together with what the reporting entity knows about the client. No single indicator is enough. The report explains the facts, the context, and why those facts led to suspicion. It should not claim that a crime has been proved.

guidance.title: What a suspicion narrative needs
guidance.text: A useful suspicion narrative answers who the client is, what they were expected to do, what actually happened, which facts are unusual, and what the reporting entity did about it. Amounts, dates, accounts, and counterparties should be traceable to the file. Public guidance asks for facts and the reasons they matter, not adjectives. If information is missing, the gap should be named rather than filled in. A threshold report such as a large cash or large virtual currency report can sit beside a suspicious transaction report, but the threshold itself is not the suspicion.

guidance.title: Virtual currency money laundering indicators
guidance.text: Public indicator material for virtual currency describes patterns that can contribute to suspicion when they do not fit the client. Examples include many wallets sending value to one client in a short time, value arriving and leaving again almost immediately, exposure to mixers or other high-risk services, and activity far above what the client described at onboarding. New addresses, chain hopping, and counterparties in higher-risk jurisdictions are further clues. Each one is an indicator. None of them proves money laundering, and ordinary clients can resemble a pattern for an innocent reason.

guidance.title: Structuring and amounts kept just below a line
guidance.text: Structuring is the pattern of breaking a sum into smaller pieces so that no single piece reaches a reporting threshold. Public indicators include repeated cash amounts just under CAD 10,000, several people delivering sub-threshold cash for one beneficiary, and a client who asks about the reporting line. The 24-hour rule can still make the combined cash reportable even when each piece stays under the line. The pattern is a reason to look. It is not, standing alone, proof that the person intended to evade a report.

guidance.title: Originator and beneficiary information on electronic transfers
guidance.text: International electronic transfers are expected to carry enough information to identify both ends. In practice that means the originator's name and account or address, and the beneficiary's name, account or address, and institution. A transfer that arrives or leaves without those fields is incomplete. The gap is a record defect to cure and, if it is deliberate or repeated, it can be one indicator among others. A missing field is not itself a suspicious transaction report, and a domestic transfer is a different control from an international one.

guidance.title: Terrorist property reports
guidance.text: A terrorist property report is about property in a reporting entity's possession or control that is owned or controlled by or on behalf of a listed person or listed entity. It is a property-reporting duty. It is not the same judgement as reasonable grounds to suspect, although the same facts can also support a suspicious transaction report. Screening against a list is how an institution notices the name. A resemblance between names is a lead. It becomes a report only when the person and the property match the legal test, which a fictional sample list cannot satisfy.

guidance.title: Politically exposed persons
guidance.text: A politically exposed person is someone who holds, or has held, a senior public office, and can include family members and close associates under the applicable definition. The public point of the control is higher inherent risk and, where the rules require it, enhanced measures: source of funds, source of wealth, and closer monitoring. Being a politically exposed person is not evidence of money laundering. A name match against a sample list is a reason to review the relationship, not a reason to file.

guidance.title: Sanctions and listed-name screening
guidance.text: Name screening compares customers and counterparties with a sanctions or listed-person list. Real programs publish official names and aliases. A practical matcher normalises case and punctuation, tolerates a missing middle name, a reordered surname, and small spelling differences, and records the score. A high score is a hit for a person to review. It is not a legal designation, and a demo system that ships a fictional list must not be treated as screening against Canadian or United Nations lists.

guidance.title: Money services business typology
guidance.text: Money services businesses move cash, wires, and often virtual currency for people who are not always the account holder. Public indicators include cash placed by one person and paid out to several others, rapid conversion from cash into another rail, and volumes that do not fit the stated business. Third-party payments are ordinary in remittance, so the indicator is the combination: many beneficiaries, weak identification, or value that does not match the declared service. The pattern supports a review. It does not establish that the business is unregistered or that the funds are illicit.

guidance.title: Casino chip and minimal-play typology
guidance.text: Casinos are reporting entities, and chips are a way to turn cash into a transferable claim. A typology described in public indicator material is the purchase of a large amount of chips, little or no actual play, and then a redemption, sometimes to another person or by a transfer off the floor. Recorded play that is only a small share of the buy-in is the fact to explain. Minimal play can also be a short visit. The indicator asks for the explanation. It does not conclude that the chips were used to launder funds.

guidance.title: Trade-based money laundering indicators
guidance.text: Trade-based money laundering hides value in the price, quantity, or quality of goods. Over-invoicing moves extra value to the seller. Under-invoicing moves extra value to the buyer. Public descriptions also include phantom shipments, where a payment has no goods, and mismatched descriptions. A useful comparison is the invoice amount against a declared customs or goods value for the same shipment. A large gap is an indicator associated with that typology. It is not proof that the trade was false, because quality, timing, and commercial terms can move a price.

guidance.title: Indicators are not determinations
guidance.text: FINTRAC publishes indicators to help reporting entities notice what may be unusual. The publications say, in substance, that a match to an indicator is not a requirement to file and is not a conclusion that money laundering or terrorist financing occurred. Context matters: the client's business, the expected volume, and whether several indicators appear together. A monitoring system should show the observed fact, the threshold it was compared with, and the transactions that are the evidence, and then leave the filing decision to a person.
